questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student claims the western Roman Empire fell in a single dramatic battle with no earlier signs of decline. What actually preceded 476 CE?
options: Centuries of gradual decline including economic trouble, invasions, and political instability
A single decisive battle that ended the empire overnight
A sudden plague that wiped out the entire Roman army
An instant surrender by the last emperor with no prior conflict
questions.answer: Centuries of gradual decline including economic trouble, invasions, and political instability
questions.why: Rome's fall was a long process, not a single event — economic troubles, repeated invasions, and weak leadership built up over centuries before 476 CE. The misconception treats it as sudden and unforeshadowed.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student says peasants (serfs) could sell their farmland whenever they wanted since they worked it every day. What's the reality?
options: Serfs did not own the land; it belonged to the lord, and serfs were tied to it
Serfs owned the land outright and could sell it freely
Serfs rented the land from the king directly
Serfs shared ownership equally with the lord
questions.answer: Serfs did not own the land; it belonged to the lord, and serfs were tied to it
questions.why: Serfs worked land owned by their lord in exchange for protection, but they had no legal ownership and couldn't leave or sell it — a key feature of the feudal system.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student says Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet purely from his own imagination with no existing story to draw from. What's wrong with this?
options: Shakespeare adapted the story from earlier sources, including an English poem by Arthur Brooke
Shakespeare copied it word-for-word from a Roman playwright
The story was based on a real historical event in London
Shakespeare wrote it as a translation of a French play
questions.answer: Shakespeare adapted the story from earlier sources, including an English poem by Arthur Brooke
questions.why: Romeo and Juliet was based on existing narrative traditions, most directly Arthur Brooke's poem 'The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet' — Shakespeare adapted rather than invented the plot.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student thinks Shakespeare only uses foreshadowing once, in the prologue, and nowhere else in the play. Which later moment also foreshadows the tragic ending?
options: Romeo's line about his 'mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars' before the Capulet party
The Nurse's joke about Juliet falling as a baby
Mercutio's pun about being a 'grave man' after being wounded
Benvolio's suggestion to go to the party to forget Rosaline
questions.answer: Romeo's line about his 'mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars' before the Capulet party
questions.why: This line directly foreshadows disaster before Romeo even meets Juliet, showing foreshadowing is woven throughout the play, not confined to the prologue's sonnet.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student thinks the love vs hate theme only appears when Romeo and Juliet speak tenderly to each other. Which moment instead shows the theme through violent conflict?
options: Tybalt's death, driven by Romeo's grief-fuelled rage after Mercutio is killed
Juliet's soliloquy waiting for Romeo on their wedding night
Romeo and Juliet's shared sonnet at the Capulet party
The Nurse's teasing about Juliet's future husband
questions.answer: Tybalt's death, driven by Romeo's grief-fuelled rage after Mercutio is killed
questions.why: The love vs hate theme is shown not just through romance but through how love (for Mercutio) fuels hate-driven violence — the feud and passion are two sides of the same emotional intensity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: In an experiment testing how the amount of sunlight affects seedling height, a student mixes up which variable is controlled. What is the controlled variable here?
options: The amount of water given to each seedling, kept the same for all
The amount of sunlight each seedling receives
The height of the seedlings at the end
The type of seedling used, which is allowed to vary
questions.answer: The amount of water given to each seedling, kept the same for all
questions.why: The controlled variable is what's kept constant so it doesn't interfere with results — here, water must stay the same while sunlight (independent) is varied and height (dependent) is measured.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: A student claims that asexual reproduction always produces offspring genetically identical to the parent, with zero exceptions ever. Is this accurate?
options: Mostly true, but mutations can still occur, so offspring aren't always a perfect genetic copy
No, asexual offspring are always completely different from the parent genetically
No, asexual reproduction always involves mixing genes from two parents
Yes, and this is also true for all sexual reproduction
questions.answer: Mostly true, but mutations can still occur, so offspring aren't always a perfect genetic copy
questions.why: Asexual reproduction produces genetically similar offspring since there's one parent, but random mutations during copying mean offspring aren't always an exact genetic clone.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student says the Crusades were fought entirely for religious reasons with no economic or political motives involved. What does this overlook?
options: Many crusaders and leaders also sought land, wealth, trade routes, and political power
The Crusades were funded entirely by the Catholic Church with no other interests
Nobles only joined for spiritual redemption and gained nothing materially
Trade was completely banned during the Crusades for religious reasons
questions.answer: Many crusaders and leaders also sought land, wealth, trade routes, and political power
questions.why: While religious motivation was central, many participants — from kings to Italian merchant cities — also pursued land, trade routes, and political gain, showing the Crusades had mixed motives.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student claims that after Rome fell, the same laws and central government simply continued under new rulers with no real change. What actually changed?
options: Centralised Roman rule was replaced by fragmented local power under feudal lords and kings
Nothing changed; Roman law codes stayed identical for centuries
The Catholic Church immediately became the only ruling government
Democracy replaced the empire across all former Roman territories
questions.answer: Centralised Roman rule was replaced by fragmented local power under feudal lords and kings
questions.why: After Rome's collapse, there was no single central authority; power fragmented into smaller kingdoms and feudal territories run by local lords rather than one unified Roman-style government.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student claims Shakespeare was primarily a novelist who occasionally dabbled in writing plays as a side hobby. What's wrong with this claim?
options: Shakespeare was first and foremost a playwright and poet, writing for the professional stage
Shakespeare never wrote poetry, only plays
Shakespeare wrote novels that were later adapted into plays by others
Shakespeare only wrote non-fiction historical accounts
questions.answer: Shakespeare was first and foremost a playwright and poet, writing for the professional stage
questions.why: Shakespeare's career centred on writing plays for performance by acting companies like the Lord Chamberlain's Men, alongside sonnets and narrative poems — not novels, which didn't exist as a form yet.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student thinks Romeo and Juliet's balcony scene uses only straightforward romantic dialogue with no wordplay or deeper technique. What technique undercuts this view?
options: Romeo's extended light/sun imagery builds a sustained metaphor elevating Juliet beyond an ordinary person
The scene is written entirely in casual prose with no poetic structure
The balcony scene contains no imagery at all, only plain statements
Juliet speaks only in questions throughout the entire scene
questions.answer: Romeo's extended light/sun imagery builds a sustained metaphor elevating Juliet beyond an ordinary person
questions.why: Romeo's 'Juliet is the sun' imagery is a sustained metaphor, a deliberate poetic technique that idealises Juliet — showing the scene is crafted with more than plain romantic talk.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A classmate argues that studying the Crusades is a waste of time in a history class focused on 'useful' skills, because nothing from that era connects to how trade, religion, or conflict work today. Explain to your classmate, using specific reasoning and at least one concrete long-term effect, why the Crusades remain relevant to understanding the modern world.
